paras.text: Carbohydrates are the most important energy containing nutrients for living organisms. Plant contains stored carbohydrates called starch while animals contain stored carbohydrates called glycogen. Both, these polymers are broken down into the simplest monosaccharide units known as glucose, before oxidation. Then glucose is oxidized in the body cells by different types of pathways (series of enzymatic chemical reactions) to release energy. This energy is stored in the form of molecules known as ATP (adenosine triphosphate) in the different parts of the body.

paras.text: Adenosine triphosphate, also known as ATP, is a molecule that carries energy within cells. It is the main energy currency of the cell and it is an end product of the processes of photophosphorylation (adding a phosphate group to a molecule using energy from light), cellular respiration and fermentation. All living things use ATP. It is also used in signal convert pathways for cell communication and is incorporated into deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) during DNA synthesis.

Polysaccharides

A polysaccharide is a complex class of carbohydrate that contains many monosaccharide units covalently bonded to each other. The number of monosaccharide units present in a polysaccharide varies from above ten units to more than hundreds units.

Polysaccharides, like disaccharides and oligosaccharides, undergo hydrolysis under appropriate conditions to produce monosaccharides.

Both cellulose and starch are naturally occurring polysaccharides that are very prevalent in the world of plants.

The paper is mainly cellulose, as is the cotton in clothing fabrics and the wood used in home construction.

Starch is a component of many types of foods, including bread, potatoes, rice, corn, beans and peas.

21.1.2 Functions

Basic function of carbohydrates is the production of energy for the performance of vital activities in living organisms. They are also known as ‘fuel of life’ because they produce energy by the process of oxidation.

These are chief sources of energy, therefore, they spare proteins and lipids for other important functions of the body. Some important functions are given below.

Glucose is used as an immediate source of energy for the sick and sportsmen. It is also used in the manufacture of jams and sweets.

Fructose is used as a sweetening agent in confectionary, in medicinal syrup. It is also used to prevent sandiness in ice-creams. It is also used as a substitute of table sugar (sucrose) for the obese and the diabetic.

Sucrose is used as a food and as ingredient of jams, jellies, confectionaries, syrup. It is also used in the preparation of sucrose octaacetate, which is used for the denaturation of alcohols and for making anhydrous adhesives.

Starch is principally used as a food. It is industrially used for manufacturing of ethanui by the process of fermentation. It is also used as a stiffening agent in textile industry and in laundry. It is also used as an adhesive to fasten paper.

Cellulose has no food value but is used as a roughage in our diet for promoting the peristaltic motion of digestive tract. It is used for the manufacturing of paper.

Oligosaccharides are involved in the formation of secreted proteins like antibodies and blood clotting factors.

The receptors on the cell membrane are the complexes of carbohydrates with certain proteins. The receptors are involved in molecular targeting or molecular recognition.

21.1.3 Nutritional Importance

Carbohydrates are the most important energy containing nutrients for living organisms. Plant contains stored carbohydrates called starch while animals contain stored carbohydrates called glycogen. Both, these polymers are broken down into the simplest monosaccharide units known as glucose, before oxidation. Then glucose is oxidized in the body cells by different types of pathways (series of enzymatic chemical reactions) to release energy. This energy is stored in the form of molecules known as ATP (adenosine triphosphate) in the different parts of the body.

Tidbit — Adenosine Triphosphate

Adenosine triphosphate, also known as ATP, is a molecule that carries energy within cells. It is the main energy currency of the cell and it is an end product of the processes of photophosphorylation (adding a phosphate group to a molecule using energy from light), cellular respiration and fermentation. All living things use ATP. It is also used in signal convert pathways for cell communication and is incorporated into deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) during DNA synthesis.

One mole of glucose on complete oxidation by citric acid cycle produces 36 ATPs.

سکروز خوراک کے طور پر اور جیم، جیلی، مٹھائیوں اور شربت کے جزو کے طور پر استعمال ہوتا ہے۔ یہ سکروز اوکٹا ایسیٹیٹ کی تیاری میں بھی استعمال ہوتا ہے، جو الکوحلز کو ناقابلِ استعمال بنانے اور بے آب چپکنے والے مادے بنانے کے لیے استعمال ہوتا ہے۔

نشاستہ بنیادی طور پر خوراک کے طور پر استعمال ہوتا ہے۔ صنعتی طور پر یہ تخمیر کے عمل سے ایتھانول کی تیاری کے لیے استعمال ہوتا ہے۔ یہ کپڑے کی صنعت اور دھلائی میں سختی دینے والے عامل کے طور پر بھی استعمال ہوتا ہے۔ کاغذ جوڑنے کے لیے یہ چپکنے والے مادے کے طور پر بھی استعمال ہوتا ہے۔

سیلولوز کی کوئی غذائی قدر نہیں لیکن یہ نظامِ ہضم کی پیرسٹالٹک حرکت کو فروغ دینے کے لیے ہماری خوراک میں ریشے کے طور پر استعمال ہوتا ہے۔ یہ کاغذ کی تیاری کے لیے استعمال ہوتا ہے۔

اولیگوسیکرائیڈز اینٹی باڈیز اور خون جمانے والے عوامل جیسے خارج ہونے والے پروٹینز کی تشکیل میں شامل ہیں۔

ایڈینوسین ٹرائی فاسفیٹ، جسے ATP بھی کہتے ہیں، ایک سالمہ ہے جو خلیوں کے اندر توانائی منتقل کرتا ہے۔ یہ خلیے کی توانائی کی بنیادی کرنسی ہے اور فوٹو فاسفوریلیشن (روشنی کی توانائی سے سالمے میں فاسفیٹ گروپ کا اضافہ)، خلوی تنفس اور تخمیر کے عمل کی آخری پیداوار ہے۔ تمام جاندار ATP استعمال کرتے ہیں۔ یہ خلوی رابطے کے سگنل راستوں میں بھی استعمال ہوتا ہے اور DNA کی تالیف کے دوران ڈی آکسی رائبونیوکلک ایسڈ (DNA) میں شامل ہو جاتا ہے۔

سٹرک ایسڈ سائیکل کے ذریعے گلوکوز کے ایک مول کی مکمل تکسید سے 36 ATP بنتے ہیں۔

Polysaccharides

A polysaccharide is a complex class of carbohydrate that contains many monosaccharide units covalently bonded to each other. The number of monosaccharide units present in a polysaccharide varies from above ten units to more than hundreds units.

Polysaccharides, like disaccharides and oligosaccharides, undergo hydrolysis under appropriate conditions to produce monosaccharides.

Both cellulose and starch are naturally occurring polysaccharides that are very prevalent in the world of plants.

The paper is mainly cellulose, as is the cotton in clothing fabrics and the wood used in home construction.

Starch is a component of many types of foods, including bread, potatoes, rice, corn, beans and peas.

21.1.2 Functions

Basic function of carbohydrates is the production of energy for the performance of vital activities in living organisms. They are also known as ‘fuel of life’ because they produce energy by the process of oxidation.

These are chief sources of energy, therefore, they spare proteins and lipids for other important functions of the body. Some important functions are given below.

Glucose is used as an immediate source of energy for the sick and sportsmen. It is also used in the manufacture of jams and sweets.

Fructose is used as a sweetening agent in confectionary, in medicinal syrup. It is also used to prevent sandiness in ice-creams. It is also used as a substitute of table sugar (sucrose) for the obese and the diabetic.

Sucrose is used as a food and as ingredient of jams, jellies, confectionaries, syrup. It is also used in the preparation of sucrose octaacetate, which is used for the denaturation of alcohols and for making anhydrous adhesives.

Starch is principally used as a food. It is industrially used for manufacturing of ethanui by the process of fermentation. It is also used as a stiffening agent in textile industry and in laundry. It is also used as an adhesive to fasten paper.

Cellulose has no food value but is used as a roughage in our diet for promoting the peristaltic motion of digestive tract. It is used for the manufacturing of paper.

Oligosaccharides are involved in the formation of secreted proteins like antibodies and blood clotting factors.

The receptors on the cell membrane are the complexes of carbohydrates with certain proteins. The receptors are involved in molecular targeting or molecular recognition.

21.1.3 Nutritional Importance

Carbohydrates are the most important energy containing nutrients for living organisms. Plant contains stored carbohydrates called starch while animals contain stored carbohydrates called glycogen. Both, these polymers are broken down into the simplest monosaccharide units known as glucose, before oxidation. Then glucose is oxidized in the body cells by different types of pathways (series of enzymatic chemical reactions) to release energy. This energy is stored in the form of molecules known as ATP (adenosine triphosphate) in the different parts of the body.

Tidbit — Adenosine Triphosphate

Adenosine triphosphate, also known as ATP, is a molecule that carries energy within cells. It is the main energy currency of the cell and it is an end product of the processes of photophosphorylation (adding a phosphate group to a molecule using energy from light), cellular respiration and fermentation. All living things use ATP. It is also used in signal convert pathways for cell communication and is incorporated into deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) during DNA synthesis.

One mole of glucose on complete oxidation by citric acid cycle produces 36 ATPs.
